summary: For children aged 7–8, build a mental map of where water is found on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, glaciers/snow/ice, and underground (and, for readier children, the atmosphere) — and tag each store as liquid or solid. Two big ideas carry the weight: water is found in many places (seen and unseen), and most of Earth's water is in the oceans. Connect frozen forms (glaciers, snow, ice) back to prior state-of-matter work: they are the same water, just solid. Keep it observational and vocabulary-rich; save proportions/percentages for a later salt-vs-fresh graphing topic.
misconceptions: 'Most water is in rivers and lakes' — not realising oceans hold the vast majority.
'Ice/snow isn't water' — not connecting frozen forms to liquid water.
'There's no water underground' — missing groundwater as a real, large store.
'All water is drinkable/fresh' — not yet distinguishing salt ocean water from fresh water (addressed fully in the later salt-vs-fresh topic).
'Water is only where you can see it' — overlooking hidden stores (groundwater, atmospheric vapour).

activities.title: Survey the cutaway Earth: tap-to-reveal water stores
steps: Look at a globe or world map and describe how much of Earth's surface is blue (ocean).
Explore a cutaway Earth scene — globe above, ground cross-section below — with water stores to discover: ocean, river, lake, mountain glacier, snowfield, and hidden groundwater below the surface.

For each store, reveal a short fact and name the store aloud: e.g. ocean → 'oceans hold most of Earth's water, and it is salty'; glacier/snowfield → 'frozen water — the same water, just solid'; below ground → 'groundwater — hidden liquid water you can't see from the surface'.
For each store, answer a lift-the-flap 'solid or liquid?' prompt before the answer is shown.
Point to or name a store you would never have guessed held water (e.g. underground).
activities.insight: Water is found in many different places — seen and unseen, solid and liquid — and the oceans hold far more than everything else combined.

activities.title: Generate and sort your own water examples
steps: Answer 'Where have YOU seen water?' and list as many places as you can (e.g. sea, puddle, tap, snow, pond, ice lolly, river).
Sort each example onto a solid-vs-liquid mat: glacier/snow/ice → solid; ocean/river/lake/puddle → liquid.
Group examples under named stores: ocean, river, lake, glacier/ice, underground, (atmosphere/clouds for readier children).
Match a store name to a photograph of that store (e.g. 'glacier' → photo of ice sheet; 'spring/well' → photo of groundwater source).
activities.insight: Every example of water belongs both to a place (store) and to a state (solid or liquid), and learners can classify their own examples, not just supplied ones.

activities.title: The jar demonstration: how much water is where
steps: Use a hands-on model where a big jar of water = the oceans, an ice cube = glaciers/ice, a spoonful = underground water, and just a drop or two = rivers and lakes.
Compare the amounts by eye and say which store holds the most.
State in your own words: 'Most of Earth's water is in the oceans; rivers and lakes are only a tiny part.'
Answer the diagnostic: 'If you gathered up ALL the water on Earth, where is most of it? And does ice count as water too?'
activities.insight: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans by a large margin; rivers and lakes are a small share; and ice is water too (solid), as is underground water.

checkQuestion: If you could gather up ALL the water on Earth — oceans, rivers, lakes, ice and underground — where is most of it? And does ice count as water too?
checkAnswer: Most of Earth's water is in the oceans (salty sea water), by far. Rivers and lakes are only a small part. Ice — glaciers, ice caps, snow — IS water, just in solid form; water can be liquid or solid. Water is also found underground.
